Exchange for breakfast: Turla's Cereal tricks are not for kids

Turla's newly discovered Cereal toolset turns a victim's Exchange server into its command-and-control system. A passive backdoor waits for encrypted commands sent through ordinary-looking OWA, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync paths. Meanwhile, a module injected into EdgeTransport.exe hooks existing transport agents to quietly copy emails and attachments involving NATO and EU addresses. ESET found the toolset at government agencies in Kazakhstan and Romania and attributed it to Turla with high confidence, noting that it never observed attacker-controlled infrastructure. Exchange admins should check for DLLs disguised as Windows components in System32\wbem, unexpected Microsoft.Exchange.*.ni.dll files in the .NET native image cache, and EdgeTransport.exe loading assemblies that aren't registered as transport agents.

Walraswap: Equilibrium-Based DEX Integrating External Liquidity

Walraswap proposes an equilibrium-based batch DEX that integrates external AMM liquidity, where a price vector exists such that all submitted orders execute with no token deficit or surplus. Unlike CoW Swap, UniswapX, and 1inch Fusion, which use uniform clearing prices alone, Walraswap's equilibrium property requires including all available trade orders, closing the solver manipulation vector where order censorship shifts clearing outcomes. DAO-elected solvers retain censorship as the sole attack surface, which the protocol treats as detectable in a repeated game (analogous to block builders not unbundling searcher bundles). The construction, originating at Flashbots in 2023, frames settlement as a convex optimization problem. Net trades at equilibrium are unique despite non-unique price vectors.
Block Time and PropAMMs: From Ethereum to Base Denim

PropAMMs face a core execution risk: the gap between an onchain quoted price and the live market rate spans one block, letting fast traders extract value at the maker's expense during that window. On Ethereum's 12-second blocks, builders such as Titan address this by guaranteeing a maker's latest price update lands before any competing trade in the same block, a mechanism Flashbots is standardizing as ERC-8324 and that Fermi has used to process hundreds of millions in weekly DEX volume. Base's Denim upgrade converts each 200ms flashblock slot into a full block, retiring the preview layer, shrinking the staleness window from 2 seconds to 200ms, and giving aggregators and solvers fresher quotes up to 2 seconds sooner. For propAMM operators, Denim makes per-block exposure limits more precise and shifts the execution advantage from tip size to sequencer latency, a dynamic Biconomy has been testing with a major market maker on its own Base propAMM since October.

Reusable Networks: Why AI Makes Crypto's Network Effects Valuable

As AI drives software production costs toward zero, value migrates from applications to the networks they compose with: protocol liquidity, on-chain identity graphs, reputation systems, and settlement rails. AI can clone interfaces and regenerate code in minutes, but it cannot reproduce the provenance of an NFT, the liquidity depth of Uniswap, or the trust accumulated in USDC. This reframes crypto's composability thesis: when any application becomes a commodity, the scarce asset is access to the shared state layer underneath. Blockchains were designed as canonical internet-layer state, and in a world where agents need reliable, permissionless coordination infrastructure, that original premise becomes a stronger value proposition.

The CFTC's approval of single-stock perpetual futures, matched by Kalshi's same-day launch, illustrates a structural trend: 2026's crypto growth concentrated in businesses treating blockchain as financial rails, while onchain-native DeFi lagged. Kalshi's architecture is representative, with orders matched in a proprietary engine and clearing running through a registered DCO, leaving blockchain to handle only stablecoin deposits/withdrawals and tokenized positions on Solana. The two growth clusters, speculation-driven (prediction markets, perps, and memecoins) and TradFi-connected (stablecoins, RWAs, and vaults), share the same pattern: platforms owning user relationships capture revenue, and blockchain captures infrastructure fees. This creates a value capture problem for the ecosystem, which risks commoditization unless more businesses emerge where blockchain is indispensable to core logic rather than settlement infrastructure.

The structural argument is that the industry will skip Stripe's intermediary layer entirely, moving from raw PANs directly to native agent token standards like VIC and AgentPay, which makes Stripe's existing network effects irrelevant. Startups that build UX around native agent token flows rather than Stripe credentials are positioned to capture agentic commerce distribution as credential ownership shifts to the card networks themselves.

The Quiet Phase: Why Active Directory Group Enumeration Deserves Your Attention

Attackers map who sits in Domain Admins with SharpHound or PowerView long before they change any group membership, and an audit entry (SACL) on the group's member attribute turns those reads into Event 4662, or 4799 for built-in groups, on the domain controller that answered. On real privileged groups, the signal drowns in reads from directory sync, Exchange, and admin tooling, and SAMR-based tools like net group /domain bypass it entirely. Pair the audit with decoy groups that nothing legitimate ever reads, correlate a decoy read and a real admin-group read from the same logon session, and check coverage with its QuietPhase PowerShell script.

CVE-2026-98432: which Linux kernels are still vulnerable

Mattias Geniar found 712 Multipath TCP listeners on his own Ubuntu 26.04 laptop, opened without his knowledge by Go programs like tailscaled, because Go 1.24 and later enable MPTCP on listening sockets by default. That matters because the only known exploit for CVE-2026-98432 needs an MPTCP listener. The bug is a use-after-free in the kernel's IPv4 TCP handshake that dates back to Linux 4.4 and can be reached with a single SYN. Upstream stable kernels were fixed in mid-October, and Debian, Amazon Linux, and Oracle UEK have shipped patches, but Ubuntu and RHEL still had no fixed kernel as of November 1.

Ephemeral Rollup: The New "L1.5" of Ethereum

A proposed "L1.5" pattern for Ethereum separates stateless compute from state by placing user secrets in wallets and commitments, nullifiers, and verifiers on L1, so rollup-style execution can run without any long-lived operator holding user state. Three forthcoming EIPs enable this: EIP-8141 frame transactions let contracts self-pay fees after verifying a proof, EIP-8250 keyed nonces repurpose privacy nullifiers to reject double spends, and EIP-8288 aggregates proofs so the block carries a single recursive proof checked once per node. Any prover can take an L1.5 job (a stateless function over L1 state and user inputs) so long as its output is checked by L1, its fee is paid without linking payer identity, and submission requires no dedicated sequencer. Target applications include gasless payments via threshold-blind-signed tickets, fair exchange for private RPC and PIR queries, and stealth privacy pools, with a three-step migration path for existing L2 apps: move owned state into wallets, enable contracts to issue their own VERIFY-frame transactions, and open proving and submission to any party.
